accuracy.evidence: Each spelling was checked against the English National Curriculum Year 2 spelling appendix: /ɔː/ spelt a before l and ll (all, ball, call, walk, talk, always), /ʌ/ spelt o (other, mother, brother, nothing, Monday), words ending -tion (station, fiction, motion, national, section) and the homophones there/their, here/hear, quite/quiet, see/sea. The a-before-l rule is stated as a strong pattern with shall and pal named as exceptions, and potion, lotion and action are standard -tion words, so nothing is overstated.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the spelling errors children make once they know a first grapheme: borl and bawl for ball (or and aw tiles with their own feedback), muther for mother (a u decoy in the build tray and m6), writing the sound shun instead of tion (shun tile, stashun option), and choosing a homophone by sound alone, such as I can here you (twin step, p3, m3, m5, m8).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtwin is built around choosing the spelling for a sound inside a whole word or sentence: a gap in b_ll that takes a, or or aw, a build tray with a u decoy for mother and Monday, a train whose end carriage must be tion, and sentence gaps that only the meaning can settle. Unlike flagaltsp, which sorts words into sound houses and reads soft c, nothing here sorts or decodes; the highest 6-token overlap with any other flagship lab is under 10%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child meets each pattern by doing it: after four gaps the a before l pattern is seen in ball, walk, talk and call before the done message states it, picking u for mother is answered with the o spelling, and the twin step gives the same sound two meanings so the sentence decides. The done text then names the rule just used.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with a tempting wrong option that the task disproves: spell ball as borl (the gap only takes a), mother with u (the tray's u is rejected), the end of station as shun (only tion hooks on) and here and hear spelled the same (the sentences need different words). The done message reports the prediction back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with shuffled options and a separate message for every wrong pick, e.g. work is a different word (a job); aw spells or in saw but before l we write a; here is a place, the listening word has ear in it; bus has u spelled u, look for an o that says u; there is a place, the lunch belongs to them so it is their.

readability.evidence: The kid explanation scores within the family limit of 5.0 and the adult text within 10.0 (validate_lessons.py). Canvas text is one short line per screen, target words are Year 2 words, and the terms phoneme, grapheme and homophone are defined in the adult notes and homophone in kid words on the twin step.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a spelling, a pattern, an exception or a mistake to watch for, with no praise padding; the explanation stays under the 12% overlap limit with Alternative Spellings for Known Sounds and the digraph lessons, and each done message states the rule just practised instead of a stock phrase.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark for every step: the b_ll gap, the five-part Monday build line and its six-tile tray fit on one row, the train engine and end carriage sit side by side, and the twin sentences wrap above and below the gap. Tiles are at least 64 px tall and the young class makes every button 56 px.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: all four tasks finish with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, and axe-core finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme. Every drag and tap has a labelled button twin, e.g. Fill b_ll with a or Add o to mother, and each result is spoken through the polite live region and the canvas aria-label.

sources: DfE (2013) English programmes of study, Key Stage 1, English Appendix 1: Spelling, Year 2 (/ɔː/ spelt a before l and ll; /ʌ/ spelt o; words ending -tion; homophones and near-homophones)
